messages.subject: Partial Migratory behaviour and variograms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Fleming,

I have a doubt in interpreting two ctmm variograms built on deers telemetry data.

For the first one (stationary individual, Fig1) I have 14 months of data and judging from the map, the deer tends to stay in the same area (about 5 km long and 1.7 km width). However it seems that the variogram in Fig 1 keeps on growing without finding athe horizontal asymptote.  This, from what I read, means that the deer is not stable in the area. However the deer occupies the same area all the time. Can I still model a stable HR even if the variogram behave like that?

The second deer (3 years of data, Fig2a and b) shows a migratory behaviour that is repeated every year as it moves for 4 months in a different area. I was thinking to cut the data, however, I would have to remove the data where the deer exhibits an exploratory behaviour (it stays in the “migration area” for a few days and then it goes back to the main area for another few days before moving in the migration area for 4 months). That would be a pity and then I would end up with 2 HRs per year rather than a general one. How would you obtain a general HR using all the data? I read the periodogram vignette and I was wondering if there was any development on the coding for the home range calculation in cases of periodic/migratory behaviour.

Thank you very much for your help

Licia

On Saturday, August 31, 2019 at 2:46:44 PM UTC-4, Teague Scott wrote:
> Hi Jenny,
>
>
> Chris might be able to answer to your question a bit more smoothly, but I'll give it a shot in the meantime.
>
> I too have run into that same error. I was using lapply() to run akde() over my telemetry object (large list of 129 objects) -  you don't need to do this. I believe that using lapply() with akde() causes it to create a unique grid for each telemetry object. I got rid of lapply() and just ran akde() on my list of telemetry objects along with my list of fits (CTMM = ). By doing this the same grid was applied to all 129 telemetry objects and I was able to run the overlap() thereafter.
>
> So don't do this:
>
> AKDES <- lapply(1:length(telem.obj), function(d){akde(telem.obj[[d]], best.fit[[d]])})
>
> Keep it simple and do this:
>
> AKDES <- akde(telem.obj, best.fit)
>
>
> Put simply, running akde() directly on a list automatically estimates akdes for all objects using the same grid.
>
> Good luck!
>
>
> - Teague
>
>

> > > dim(UDList2[[2]][["PDF"]])
> >   x   y

> >

If differing PDF dimensions for each fitted UD is what is causing the wrror, is there a way to standardize the dimensions of the PDFs so that I can calculate UD overlap? (Incidentally, I noticed that the functions calls for "aligned UDs." How does one ensure they are getting aligned UDs?) Alternatively, is there something else that could be causing the error?
> >
> > Many thanks in advance,
> > Jenny Hansen

messages.subject: Re: Partial Migratory behaviour and variograms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Licia,

For deer 1, if I had to guess, they are probably exhibiting multi-scale behavior where they use a small transient range that moves around within the larger 5 x 1.7 km^2 range. I've seen this with deer and elephants. The multi-scale models required are not yet in the package, and probably will not be for a couple of years. Alternatively, there could be some issue with data quality (such as bursts of high frequency sampling) that requires an error model or thinning the data down to where the error doesn't matter.

For deer 2, the ideal analysis is not yet implemented, but what I would do to approximate it is to segment the data in to 3 behaviors (summer, winter, migration), and then for each behavior (and using all years if there is fidelity) estimate the ranging area, and then average the 3 ranges together with the mean() function. I need to update the CIs for that calculation, but the point estimate should be good.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
messages.subject_clean: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
A reviewer recommended this package to expand the analysis in my manuscript beyond Minimum Convex Polygon. After playing around with the package and reading the various supporting material, now I'm not so sure that my dataset lends itself to this analysis. I manually radio-tracked tortoises and recorded observations via GPS. Tracking duration ranged from 4-6 months, in which time I obtained 29-50 fixes on each individual. Intervals between fixes ranged between 2~6 days. Individuals did exhibit fidelity to certain areas, although repeat observations in the same location may not represent 'autocorrelation' in the same sense that two fixes one hour apart do.

I see that the timestamp is a necessary datum for each fix, and upon examining the 'Buffalo' dataset, I noticed the timestamp values range between 5:00~59:00. Being unfamiliar with this type of tracking and MoveBank, it doesn't seem like the date is associated with each fix, is that correct? Does the package take into account the date and time of the fix, or just the time (i.e., is the autocorrelation that is being addressed only across the span of a couple of hours within the same day)?

Thank you for any comments directed toward my specific situation and in satisfying my general curiosity in the package.

Ross Couvillon

Dear Chris,

Thank you very much fo your quick reply.
For deer 1 data quality is not too bad I think, I have a few gaps of 1 day every 1-2 months and a big gap of 5 days. The deer was probably in some area with poor GPS coverage. It could be a multiscale bahaviour as you said I think. In such case, can I still use the ctmm function ?or would you suggest another method?

For deer 2, I did what you suggested and the variogram for area 1 (split1variogram_full, calculated using only the area 1 locations pooling all years together) seems OK but in area 2 (split2variogram_full) there are temporal gaps, occurring because I've truncated te data. Are these gaps affecting the winter HR estimation? Can I use this variogram to calculate the 3-years winter HR? I'm a bit concerned that the model would give more "weight" or importance to the locations at the beginning and at the end of the wintering period. I'm not sure if it's clear what I'm trying to say... Does the mean() function average only the areas or it also acts on the perimeter of them?

Thanks a lot again!

Best Regards

Licia

messages.subject: Re: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
messages.subject_clean: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

I don't know what species you are working with, but I know from experience that both Sonoran and Galapogos tortoises take a couple of weeks to cross their range, and so for them a 2-6 day sampling interval would give rise to some autocorrelation.

When autocorrelation is not present in the data, home-range analysis in ctmm automatically reduces to an IID KDE, but with a couple of bias corrections that will help with smaller sample sizes (29-50 fixes is small for nonparametric methods like KDE and MCP). Even with IID data, the default method in ctmm is more statistically efficient than conventional KDE methods used in ecology, so there's still a benefit to using it. You can also account for telemetry error in ctmm, which can be important in some datasets regardless of autocorrelation.

The full date-time is used in ctmm. You might be looking at a dataset from another R package. Try data('buffalo',package='ctmm') or without capitalizing 'buffalo'. Autocorrelation timescales can be of any duration. The package has been tested on species from bacterium to whales. Everything is rescaled internally for numerical stability and output units can range from microns to kilometers.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Partial Migratory behaviour and variograms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Licia,

Gaps make the variogram ugly, but are not generally a problem otherwise. What can throw the model off (when error is not included) is short bursts or tiny timesteps in the data.

If I had to use data like deer 1, I would look to segment the data (if there are discrete shifts) or do a sliding window analysis (if there is continuous shifting) and aggregate the transient ranges together.

The mean() function averages the density functions, but corresponding CIs are not currently estimated with any rigor, so let me know if you need that implemented beforehand.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Convergence in path simulations etc.
messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

hope you are doing well. I contacted you via the ctmm usergroup forum a while ago, having some questions regarding behaviour-based path simulations. messages.subject: Re: Convergence in path simulations etc.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ines,

Nice to hear from you.

1.) As for convergence, let me talk about the mean "time spent", T, because its easier to discuss concretely, but you can also use the median. For an ensemble of N simulations, you have an estimate of the mean "time spent", E[T], and an estimate of the variance of "time spent", VAR[T]. But you only have estimates, so they have uncertainty associated with N being finite. In the normal approximation, the variance of the estimate of E[T] is just VAR[T]/N, which slowly improves by increasing N. Because T is positive, what I do in the speed() function, which is very analogous to this, is to a priori target a relative error for the ratio of the standard error sqrt(VAR[T]/N) and E[T]. Then I can say something like "this is my numerical estimate of E[T], which I've calculated well enough to have only one part in one hundred numerical error, on average".

2.) Different datasets might converge to the same numerical-error threshold at different rates. I would target a meaningful amount of numerical error rather than a number of simulations.

3.) I'm not sure that I follow this question. Your ensemble of simulated trajectories gives you an ensemble of time spent in habitat, which you can summarize by statistics or model with a distribution.

4.) In my opinion, the advantages I see for doing this kind of analysis with conditional simulations rather than raw location estimates are (1) you can account for telemetry error (I can't recall if you modeled that); (2) you can account for differences and or irregularities in the sampling rates; (3) you can place confidence intervals on what habitats were used during the observation period. The disadvantages I see are that you are assuming the movement model is not strongly influenced by habitat. For instance, small fish near the shore will have some simulations that cross land even though they never do that.

We have paper on the speed() function in review that is the most similar to this kind of analysis, but its still in review. What you cite is probably the best reference, second to that.

Best,
Chris

Hi Lorena,

1.) That variogram looks very resident, so yes. After the initial increase, you can imagine a flat line going through all of that noise.
2.) I'm not exactly sure what your question is, but vignette('periodogram') covers periodic model selection. Periodograms are not going to be super insightful when there is periodicity in the collection of the data, which is what the diagnostic is for, and yours have peaks.

What steps to take after vignette('variogram') and vignette('akde'), etc.? I think that depends on what your research questions are. There is other functionality in the ctmm package, like speed() and overlap(). You can do post-hoc analysis on the results. There are also important movement analyses that are not in the ctmm package, like RSFs and SSFs.

Best,

messages.subject: tau_v and 95% decay in velocity autocorrelation
messages.subject_clean: tau_v and 95% decay in velocity autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Based on earlier discussion, I understand that if I have an OUF model and I want to know the time interval at which there is a 95% decay in velocity correlation, I would use the following formula:

tau_v * -log(0.05)

this is close to tau_v * 3

I have a few questions about this calculation. Given the following:

t <- a telemetry object
v <- a variogram
m <- an ouf model

tv_min <- m$tau['velocity']/60
nov_min <- m$tau['velocity'] * -log(0.05)/60

plot(v,CTMM=m, xlim=c(0,2 %#% "hour"))
abline(v=tv_min/60,col='red')
abline(v=nov_min/60,col='blue')

First, how do I interpret the value of tau_v (here it is ~13 min)? I had thought that tau_v (red line) is the point at which velocity is uncorrelated, but that is incorrect. Instead, tau_v * 3 (blue line) is the point at which velocity is mostly uncorrelated. So, why do I need to multiply by 3?

Second, why do I need to perform -log() to get the correct value? I.e. tau_v has to be multiplied by -log(0.05), and not simply 0.95 to get the correct value.

Thanks a lot for your help!

Ben

messages.subject: Re: tau_v and 95% decay in velocity autocorrelation
messages.subject_clean: tau_v and 95% decay in velocity autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

tau_velocity is approximately the timescale over which correlations in velocity decay exponentially. Velocity autocorrelation decays with an envelope like exp(-lag/tau_velocity). So when only 5% of velocity autocorrelation is remaining you have 0.05=exp(-lag/tau_velocity) which you can solve to find  lag=-log(0.05)*tau_velocity.

But also for this specific variogram, I would be careful to make sure that telemetry error or non-stationarity aren't problematic because the fitted model is only nailing the first lag. The sampling rate seems to be ~5 minutes. With larger species, the finer the sampling, the bigger problem unmodeled telemetry error becomes for underestimating tau_velocity.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Using mixed models with the Fit output
messages.subject_clean: Using mixed models with the Fit output
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kyana,

summary() on the model fit returns a Gaussian area estimate at the specified quantile level.UD, while summary() on the AKDE returns a non-parametric area estimate at the specified quantile level.UD. If the distribution is not Gaussian, then summary() on the model fit still has meaning as (proportional to) variance in locations. Exploratory bouts get picked up in the tails of the distribution (higher quantiles).

It is more reasonable to feed the estimates (and their variances from the diagonal of slot COV) into a meta-analysis like with R package metafor, but at some point this kind of functionality will be in the package.

Different habitats is good for checking the veracity of the DOP/error estimates, though I expect the e-obs error estimates to be okay. Multiple devices is also a good idea.
N=24 locations is not very much for a calibration dataset, unless you have like 20 tags and they all behave identically. Relative error in the calibration parameter is like 1/sqrt(N), so you want a few hundred locations in total or per device, depending on how similar they behave.
I'm very interested in looking at more calibration data by October 13th, for a manuscript on telemetry error.

Best,
Chris

I believe that using lapply() with akde() causes it to create a unique grid for each telemetry object. By doing this the same grid was applied to all 129 telemetry objects and I was able to run the overlap() thereafter.

> > Keep it simple and do this:
> >
> > AKDES <- akde(telem.obj, best.fit)
> >
> >
> > Put simply, running akde() directly on a list automatically estimates akdes for all objects using the same grid.
